3c1e2a86bf2a86cd: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 30 — Malaysian action film Chelot has hit RM19.5 million at the box office as of September 27, with director Adrian Teh confirming that a sequel is now in development.
The announcement was made on Monday at Bonda Kuala Lumpur in Kampung Baru during a celebration marking the film’s box-office performance, where Teh declared: “Chelot 2 is a go.”
The sequel remains in its early stages, with work currently focused on the script.
No shooting or release date has been announced, while details on whether the original cast will return remain up in the air.
The RM19.5 million haul puts Chelot second among the highest-grossing Malaysian films of 2026, behind Tarung: Unforgiven, which has collected RM23.3 million.

Polong is currently third with RM15 million, followed by Bobby Husaini’s Libang Libu with RM14.1 million and Nazifdin Nasrudin’s Malaikat Malam with RM12.2 million, rounding out the top five local films to have crossed the RM10 million mark this year.
Chelot has drawn particular praise for its action sequences, 95 per cent of which were achieved using practical effects rather than CGI.
Its standout set piece is a single-take action sequence recognised by the Malaysia Book of Records as the longest of its kind in Malaysian cinematic history.

Produced by ACT 2 Pictures, Golden Screen Cinemas (GSC), Astro Shaw, SunStrong Entertainment and Marvellous Culture & Film, Chelot features an ensemble cast led by Beto Kusyairy, Shukri Yahaya, Shaheizy Sam, Nadhir Nasar, Alicia Amin, Mustaqim Bahadon and Theebaan G.
The film follows special operations police officer Inspector Haqqim (Shukri), who is struggling with debt and family pressure.
After a high-stakes raid goes tragically wrong, he secretly becomes an informant for a dangerous weapons-smuggling ring led by Datuk Bakri (Shaheizy) and his right-hand man Azraf (Beto).
Haqqim finds himself caught between his duties as a police officer and the criminal underworld, forcing him into a dangerous game in which his loyalties are constantly tested.
Chelot is still screening in cinemas nationwide.
19283035b8ad284d: MANCHESTER, Sept 30 — Manchester City face severe sanctions after being found guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules over a nine-season period.

Abu Dhabi-backed City were found to have arranged “sham” contracts with a number of commercial partners to artificially inflate the club’s revenues and reduce costs by more than £900 million (RM4.85 billion) between 2009 and 2018.
In doing so they concealed the true state of their finances and avoided breaches of Premier League and Uefa spending limits as a result.
An independent commission also found the club guilty on the majority of charges in relation to their failure to co-operate with the league’s investigation.
No sanction has yet been imposed and City said they will appeal against the decision.
But the ruling will send shockwaves through English football, with City’s place in the Premier League now at risk and questions over whether titles could be stripped.

“The core decision establishes the facts of what happened at Manchester City during this period. It details how the club systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade,” Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said in a statement on Tuesday.
“This disciplinary case, and this decision, are the most significant in Premier League history.
“Now we have the commission’s decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the league, our clubs and fans.”
The commission found City arranged commercial deals whereby companies were only required to pay a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees.
The remainder was funded by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan’s Abu Dhabi United Group Investment and Development (ADUG), which owned the club.
Further arrangements, funded by ADUG, enabled the club to record lower operating expenses than they actually incurred.
As a result, City failed to accurately report income and expenditure for the purposes of the Premier League and Uefa’s financial sustainability rules.

The scheme was found to have inflated revenue by more than £830 million, while income from image rights was over-stated by almost £74 million, with liabilities for staff contracts under-stated by nearly £17 million.
The commission found they would have breached spending limits “by a very substantial amount” if City had reported accurately.
City set to appeal
In addition, City were found to have “made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the Premier League” during a four-year investigation.
The commission found that evidence given by several important factual witnesses on behalf of City was “false in a number of key respects”.
It added that “certain of those factual witnesses had given evidence at the hearing that they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest”.
“It’s incredibly serious, the Premier League report is incredibly stark,” said the British government’s culture, media and sport secretary Lisa Nandy.
Since a 2008 takeover from Sheikh Mansour, vice-president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates, City have become the Premier League’s dominant force.
They have won eight Premier League titles, four FA Cups and seven League Cups over the past 15 years and also won the Champions League for the first time in 2023.
But that same year they were hit by the Premier League with over 100 charges following an investigation into alleged breaches of rules.
The hearing by an independent commission started in September 2024 and concluded three months later.
City expressed “surprise” at the decision and vowed to continue fighting to clear their name.

“Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe,” the club said in a statement.
According to Premier League rules, the sanction can vary from a points deduction, a fine or even expulsion from the division.
Everton and Nottingham Forest were handed points deductions in the 2023/24 season for single breaches of financial sustainability rules.
On that basis, City would face likely relegation if the same penalty is applied for each of the over 100 charges.
“If the appeal fails, Manchester City cannot stay in the league, they have to suffer. And I say that as a supporter and a fan,” said the club’s former chairman David Bernstein. — AFP

fd8ce776b3a03e4a: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 30 — Bursa Malaysia’s key index rebounded to open higher on Wednesday as bargain hunting emerged after recent losses, despite negative cues from Wall Street.
At 9.10am, the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI (FBM KLCI) recovered 4.34 points, or 0.26 per cent, to 1,648.30 from Tuesday’s close of 1,643.96.
The index opened 2.53 points higher at 1,646.49.
On the broader market, decliners outpaced gainers 214 to 174. A total of 293 counters were unchanged, 2,174 untraded and 95 suspended.
Turnover stood at 265.65 million shares worth RM151.82 million.

Rakuten Trade Sdn Bhd vice-president of equity research Thong Pak Leng said the market is increasingly oversold, creating opportunities for selective accumulation in fundamentally sound blue-chip stocks.
Any recovery, however, will likely remain narrow unless foreign selling moderates and banking heavyweights regain support, he said.
“Energy, renewable infrastructure and selected defensive counters may outperform, while technology stocks remain vulnerable to high global yields.
“Thus, we expect a cautious session, with bargain hunting around 1,640, placing the index within the 1,635-1,655 range,” he told Bernama.

Among the heavyweights, Maybank rose three sen to RM10.02, Public Bank gained two sen to RM4.74, while CIMB fell two sen to RM7.76. Tenaga Nasional added 10 sen to RM12.82, and IHH Healthcare was flat at RM7.87.

In active trade, Zetrix AI added half a sen to 17 sen, V.S Industry recouped 1.5 sen to 25 sen, Visdynamics expanded 10 sen to 52 sen, while Cuscapi remained unchanged at five sen and Gamuda earned 13 sen to RM5.11.

Among the top gainers, Allianz Malaysia and MISC both advanced 14 sen to RM21 and RM7.74, respectively. Hong Leong Industries inched up 10 sen to RM16.60, MI Technovation and UMS Integration both firmed nine sen to RM5.48 and RM8.70, respectively.

Eurospan led the top losers, falling 29 sen to RM2.95, Petronas Dagangan shed 28 sen to RM19.04, Aeon Credit edged down 14 sen to RM5.05, while Dutch Lady and Hong Leong Bank erased 12 sen each to RM29.88 and RM23.16, respectively.
On the index board, the FBM Mid 70 Index fell 21.36 points to 17,588.72, the FBM Emas Index climbed 19.22 points to 12,284.69, and the FBM Top 100 Index improved 19.81 points to 12,071.35.
The FBM Emas Shariah Index ticked up 25.02 points to 12,152.63, and the FBM ACE Index trimmed 4.12 points to 5,524.46.

Sector-wise, the Industrial Products and Services Index slipped 0.36 of-a-point to 180.50, while the Energy Index gave up 4.42 points to 864.28. The Financial Services Index perked up 10.43 points to 19,271.29, while the Plantation Index added 1.86 points to 9,218.20. — Bernama
259f9e9afc586601: SEPTEMBER 30 — In the case of Re Datuk James Wong Kim, Minister of Home Affairs, Malaysia & Ors v Datuk James Wong Kim Min [1976], the legality of a detention order came before the Federal Court on appeal from the High Court.

The detention order was made under a regulation of the Preservation of Public Security Regulations (PPSR) which was made under the Preservation of Public Security Ordinance 1962 (PPSO). The PPSO was enacted by the Sarawak Legislature before Malaysia Day.

The issue in the appeal was whether or not the Federal Secretary, Sarawak could lawfully, under a regulation of PPSR, by order direct a detainee to be detained when at the time of the order the detainee was outside Sarawak.

In a unanimous decision, the apex court dismissed the appeal, holding that the PPSO, although declared to be a federal law, continued to have effect only in Sarawak. The three judges each deliver a separate judgment.
In the course of his judgment, Lord President Suffian explained the lawfulness of the PPSO and PPSR as follows:

“Before Malaysia Day the Sarawak legislature had power to make law on internal security. So the PPSO and PPSR were perfectly valid, but it is clear that the detaining authority in Sarawak could not then order a person to be detained outside Sarawak.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This file picture shows the Sarawak State Legislative Assembly building in Kuching, December 3, 2025. — Bernama pic

“After Malaysia Day however when Sarawak ceased to be a Crown Colony and became independent as a member state of Malaysia, Sarawak became voluntarily subject to the Malaysian constitution and under this constitution internal security is a federal subject, so that both legislative and executive authority over internal security is now vested in the Federation and in particular the Sarawak legislature no longer has power to make law on it. (See item 3, List I in the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution).

“But the advent of Malaysia Day did not however automatically repeal the Sarawak laws; on the contrary they were expressly saved by Section 73 of the Malaysia Act, which by subsection (5) provides that the Sarawak laws were ‘present laws’ and by subsection (1) that ‘they shall, on and after Malaysia Day, have effect according to their tenor, and be construed as if this Act had not been passed’.

“Further by subsection (3), the Section provides that as these Sarawak laws cannot be passed after Malaysia Day by the Sarawak legislature they ‘shall, on and after Malaysia Day, be treated as federal laws’.

“[Subsection] (1) of Section 73 which saved them from automatic repeal expressly says … that on and after Malaysia Day they shall have effect according to their tenor and as if the Malaysia Act had not been passed, i.e. within Sarawak only, as was the case before Malaysia Day. If that were not so, there would have been no necessity for Section 74 of the Malaysia Act, of which subsections (1) and (2) provide:

“(1) Subject to the provisions of this Section the Yang Di-Pertuan Agong may by order make such modifications as appear to him to be necessary or expedient in consequence of the passing of this Act in any present law relating to matters [such as internal security] about which Parliament has power to make laws.

“(2) Subject to subsection (3), the power to make orders under subsection (1) shall include power to extend throughout Malaysia or to any State or States thereof any present law in force in any part of Malaysia about any such matter; but except in consequence of the extension of any present law no such order shall modify any State law (this subsection is given as amended by Act 31/65).

“It is clear from these provisions that any Sarawak law passed before Malaysia Day on a matter which on and after Malaysia Day became a matter concerning which Parliament (not the Sarawak legislature) has power to make law, on and after Malaysia Day remains good law, but it continues to have effect only within Sarawak.
“[T]he Yang Di-Pertuan Agong may by order make such modifications as may appear to him necessary or expedient in that law, and this royal power includes power to extend throughout Malaysia that law.”
The second judge, Chief Justice of Borneo (as it was formerly known) Lee Hun Hoe too took time to explain the PPSO and PPSR. In the course of his judgment, the learned Chief Justice said as follows:

“In 1946 Sarawak became a Crown Colony after more than a century under Brooke Rule. The PPSO was enacted by the Council Negri (State Legislature) and came into force on May 18, 1962. Its operation was limited to Sarawak and had no extra-territorial effect. There were only eight sections.

“On December 8, 1962, the Governor declared the provisions of Section 4(2) to come into operation (See Part II of the Sarawak Government Gazette Notification No. S.220/62). Pursuant to Section 4 the Governor, on the same day, made the PPSR and the Preservation of Public Security (Detention Orders) Rules. The PPSO and subsidiary legislation made thereunder therefore remained in force when Sarawak joined Malaysia on September 16, 1963. This was also the operative date of the Malaysia Act, 1963. (See Federal Government Gazette L.N. No. 214/63).

“With the formation of Malaysia certain matters previously under State Control were transferred to Federal Control and listed under the Ninth Schedule of the Federal Constitution under Federal List. One of these matters is internal security which includes police, prisons, preventive detention, restriction of residence and so forth.

“By virtue of the Modification of Laws (Internal Security and Public Order) (Borneo States) Order 1963 certain present laws applicable to Malaya and enumerated under the First Schedule to the Order were extended to Sabah and Sarawak and called ‘the extension laws’. One of these is the Internal Security Act, 1960.
“In the same way, certain present laws of Sabah and Sarawak specified in the Second Schedule of the Order continued to have effect in the two States as ‘the continuing laws’.

“On May 25, 1965, the Yang Di-Pertuan Agong with the concurrence of the Governor in the exercise of his powers under Section 74 of the Malaysia Act made the Modification of Laws (Declaration of Federal Present Laws) (Sarawak) Order 1965 to come into force on Malaysia Day (see F.L.N. 200 of 1965) … under which State statutory instruments were declared to be federal laws … [including] the PPSO and subsidiary legislation made thereunder.”

According to the learned Chief Justice, to determine the legal effect of the PPSO and PPSR, it necessitated “looking into relevant provisions of the Malaysia Act, 1963 and of the Federal Constitution”.
The most appropriate provision to begin with is Article 159A of the Federal Constitution which reads as follows:

“The provisions of Part IV of the Malaysia Act (which contains temporary and transitional provisions in connection with the operation of that Act) shall have effect as if embodied in this Constitution, and shall have effect notwithstanding anything in this Constitution as amended by that Act; and the provisions of this Constitution, and in particular Clause (1) of Article 4 and Articles 159 and 161E shall have effect in relation thereto accordingly.”
Part IV of the Malaysia Act 1963 commences with Section 73 dealing with the continuation and effect of ‘present laws’. Section 74 deals with the temporary power to modify and apply present laws.
After setting out the provisions in extenso, the learned Chief Justice ruled that “the PPSO and subsidiary legislation made thereunder were ‘present laws’ of Sarawak” and declared federal laws.

The learned Chief Justice then cited the case of Assa Singh v Mentri Besar of Johore where the Federal Court held that the Restricted Residence Enactment, a pre-Merdeka law, must be applied with the necessary modifications to bring it into accord with the Federal Constitution.
The above explains further the legal effect of the laws of Sabah and Sarawak passed or made before Malaysia Day.

Article 159A of the Federal Constitution clearly states that Part IV of the Malaysia Act 1963 (which contains temporary and transitional provisions in connection with the operation of that Act) shall be embodied in the Federal Constitution.

The determination of the legal effect of the present laws of Sabah and Sarawak — that is, the laws of passed or made before Malaysia Day — such as the Oil Mining Ordinance 1958 (Sarawak) and Mining Ordinance 1960 (Sabah), necessitates looking into Article 159A of the Federal Constitution, among others, and Part IV of the Malaysia Act 1963.
* This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
377acc34b66e9877: PETALING JAYA: Former prime minister Dr Mahathir Mohamad has been admitted to the National Heart Institute (IJN) to be placed under observation, says his son, Mukhriz.
Mukhriz said the 101-year-old was admitted to IJN yesterday, Bernama reported.
A spokesman for Mahathir’s office, Sufi Yusoff, said the former prime minister was well and resting at IJN.
Mahathir’s wife, Dr Hasmah Ali, died at IJN on Monday morning at the age of 100. She was accorded a state funeral and laid to rest at Pusara Negara in Putrajaya.
Her death was followed by a wave of tributes, with many highlighting her warmth and grace as well as her contributions to the nation.
Mahathir said he was not expecting Hasmah to die as she appeared well the day before.
Mahathir has a history of heart ailments and underwent heart bypass operations in 1989 and 2007.
In January, he suffered a hip fracture after a fall at home. He underwent physiotherapy treatment instead of going for a surgery due to his age.
376ec9236481d980: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 30 — A former director-general (DG) of the Federal Land Development Authority (Felda) was charged at the Sessions Court here today with deceiving the authority’s board of directors in connection with a power of attorney used to transfer the ownership of 16 parcels of its land at Jalan Semarak in 2014.
Datuk Faizoull Ahmad, 66, however, pleaded not guilty after the charge was read out before Judge Suzana Hussin.

Faizoull, in his capacity as Felda DG, is accused of deceiving the board by concealing a power of attorney dated June 3, 2014, granted Synergy Promenade Sdn Bhd authority to transfer ownership of the 16 parcels of land involved in the proposed Felda Lot Development Project at Jalan Semarak.

The act induced the board of directors to agree to the power of attorney, resulting in the transfer of ownership of the said Felda land to Synergy Promenade KLVC Sdn Bhd and Synergy Promenade Sdn Bhd, when the Board would not have done so had it not been deceived.
The offence is alleged to have been committed at the Board Meeting Room, Level 50, Menara Felda, Platinum Park, Persiaran KLCC here on Sept 2, 2014.
He was charged under Section 420 of the Penal Code, which carries a prison sentence of between one and 10 years and caning, as well as a fine, upon conviction. — Bernama

18daffc55483bc40: SINGAPORE: The dollar stood near this year's high versus the euro on Wednesday and was poised for the largest monthly rise against it for 14 months, powered by US growth and rising US interest rates in contrast to the energy and debt worries swirling in Europe.
Overnight, the euro dipped to its lowest since May 2025, at US$1.1312, and traded nearby at US$1.1339 in Asia. The euro is also testing support around 178 yen.
Through September the dollar is up nearly 2.5% on the euro, and the rising greenback also pushed its Australian counterpart below 70 cents for the first time since early August.

"The US economy is running hot, Europe is losing the global AI race, and energy supplies and French politics remain big concerns for the euro," said Brent Donnelly, president of foreign exchange trading at analytics firm Spectra Markets.
Earlier this month benchmark European gas prices spiked to their highest since 2022.

French markets are under pressure from debt and political gridlock, ahead of next year's presidential election, and the spread with German yields has blown beyond 115 basis points to its widest since 2012.

The skew in options prices has tipped sharply in recent sessions to favour buying protection against further euro falls - though Donnelly says the dollar probably needs strong US data to make further headway from here.

The dollar also made a 16-1/2-month top on the Swiss franc overnight at 0.8358 francs. The franc has suffered, in part, because investors have gone looking for low-yielding alternatives to yen to sell in search of carry elsewhere.

The yen has fallen out of favour as a short against the dollar following US-Japan yen buying in July and August, which has been followed by warnings not to test their resolve, as well as a pickup in the pace of Japanese rate hikes.
The dollar has fallen 1.5% on the yen in September.

The Fed's preferred inflation yardstick, US core PCE, is due out later on Wednesday though the market is focused on Friday's US jobs report which, if strong, could reinforce expectations that US interest rates are on the rise.

Some of those expectations took a hit overnight when influential New York Fed president John Williams said there is "no need for urgency" in raising rates. Two-year Treasury yields fell about 3.5 basis points and Fed funds futures pricing for a rate hike next month dialled back to 50% from 71%.

Australian inflation figures due later on Wednesday could lend support to the Aussie, which slipped after Reserve Bank of Australia governor Michele Bullock said the board discussed holding rates before announcing Tuesday's 25-bp hike.

"The risk is another hike by the RBA, possibly as soon as the next policy meeting in November. However, another hike is already priced in by markets," said Commonwealth Bank of Australia's head of foreign exchange, Joe Capurso.

"We still consider the next big move in AUD/USD is down not up," he said. The Australian dollar hovered around US$0.6986 early in the Asia session, 20 pips above its overnight low, and the New Zealand dollar, which hit its lowest since last November overnight, was pinned at US$0.5638.

Sterling touched a three-month trough on Tuesday and last sat nearby at US$1.3227. The yuan headed for its seventh straight quarterly gain on the dollar in its final session before China's Oct 1-7 holidays.

96b8733b678ca1a7: The Sedition Act 1948 ought to be struck out unless Parliament amends the Federal Constitution to expressly incorporate it as a permitted restriction on free speech.
A colonial relic, the Sedition Act was enacted when the country was under imperial control.

It has survived almost 70 years since Merdeka not because of constitutional legitimacy but due to judicial pronouncements rooted in the outdated notion that Malaysia practised parliamentary supremacy.

That principle, prevailing in the UK, holds that Parliament has the ultimate legal authority to enact, amend or repeal any law, and that no other institution, not even the courts, has the power to override or invalidate its legislation.

On that basis, the Sedition Act had for decades lingered as a convenient instrument of state authority, defended on the premise that Parliament may restrict speech absolutely in the name of national security.
Since 2017, however, the Federal Court has firmly embraced constitutional supremacy, and under this doctrine, the Sedition Act can no longer stand.
Constitutional supremacy dictates that the Federal Constitution is the supreme law of the land. Any legislation, whether pre- or post-Merdeka, that conflicts with its spirit must be voided.
Article 10(2)(a) of the constitution permits restrictions on free speech, but only if they are reasonable and proportionate.
The Sedition Act fails this test.
Predating the constitution itself, it criminalises speech based on vague notions of “seditious tendency”, without requiring proof of intent to incite violence or disorder.
Such a law bypasses constitutional safeguards and undermines the very liberties the constitution guarantees.
The judiciary’s oath of office, prescribed by the constitution itself, provides further clarity. Judges do not swear allegiance to Parliament or the government of the day.
Their solemn oath is to preserve, protect and defend the constitution.

Judicial power, vested in the superior courts by the constitution, is not a passive instrument to rubber-stamp legislative excess. It is an active and inherent power that allows the courts to act as the ultimate check and balance.

When a law infringes upon fundamental liberties, the judiciary has a constitutional duty to intervene. To leave the Sedition Act intact merely because it has been historically preserved is to betray that oath.
The jurisprudential shift taken by the apex court leaves no room for ambiguity. The courts must now exercise their full constitutional judicial power to strike down the Sedition Act.
Doing so will dismantle a vestige of colonial control and affirm Malaysia’s commitment to governance under its own constitution.
The judiciary will also be viewed not merely as honouring its oath but as fulfilling the nation’s promise to uphold the true supremacy of its constitution.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
3bb7b621384ec666: Akta Hasutan 1948 wajar dibatalkan melainkan Parlimen meminda Perlembagaan Persekutuan untuk secara jelas membenarkan akta itu sebagai satu bentuk sekatan terhadap kebebasan bersuara.
Akta Hasutan adalah tinggalan penjajah yang digubal ketika negara masih berada di bawah pemerintahan British.

Ia kekal hampir tujuh dekad selepas merdeka bukan kerana keabsahannya dari sudut Perlembagaan, tetapi kerana keputusan mahkamah yang menurut pandangan saya berasaskan tanggapan lapuk bahawa Malaysia mengamalkan prinsip ketertinggian Parlimen.

Prinsip yang diamalkan di United Kingdom itu meletakkan Parlimen sebagai badan perundangan tertinggi yang mempunyai kuasa muktamad untuk menggubal, meminda atau memansuhkan undang-undang, tanpa institusi lain termasuk mahkamah boleh mengetepikannya.
Atas asas itu, Akta Hasutan bertahan sekian lama sebagai salah satu instrumen kuasa negara, dengan sekatan terhadap kebebasan bersuara dipertahankan atas alasan keselamatan negara.

Namun, sejak 2017 Mahkamah Persekutuan memberikan penekanan lebih jelas terhadap keluhuran Perlembagaan dan kuasa kehakiman. Berdasarkan perkembangan ini, pada pandangan saya, kedudukan Akta Hasutan perlu dinilai semula.

Keluhuran Perlembagaan bermakna Perlembagaan Persekutuan adalah undang-undang tertinggi negara. Undang-undang yang tidak selaras dengannya tidak boleh mengatasi jaminan yang diberikan oleh Perlembagaan.
Perkara 10(2)(a) membenarkan Parlimen mengenakan sekatan terhadap kebebasan bersuara atas alasan tertentu, termasuk keselamatan negara, ketenteraman awam dan moral.
Pada pandangan saya, Akta Hasutan tidak memenuhi piawaian yang sewajarnya bagi menyekat kebebasan tersebut.

Akta yang wujud sebelum Perlembagaan itu menjadikan sesuatu ucapan sebagai kesalahan berdasarkan konsep 'kecenderungan menghasut', tanpa perlu membuktikan bahawa seseorang mempunyai niat untuk mencetuskan keganasan atau kekacauan.
Keadaan itu, pada pandangan saya, boleh menjejaskan perlindungan terhadap kebebasan yang dijamin oleh Perlembagaan.
Sumpah jawatan hakim yang ditetapkan dalam Perlembagaan turut memberi panduan mengenai tanggungjawab badan kehakiman.
Hakim tidak mengangkat sumpah untuk taat kepada Parlimen atau kerajaan yang memerintah.
Sebaliknya, mereka bersumpah untuk memelihara, melindungi dan mempertahankan Perlembagaan.

Kuasa kehakiman bukan sekadar untuk menerima setiap tindakan perundangan tanpa penelitian. Mahkamah memainkan peranan penting dalam memastikan tindakan badan perundangan dan eksekutif kekal dalam batas Perlembagaan.
Apabila sesuatu undang-undang didakwa menjejaskan kebebasan asasi, badan kehakiman mempunyai tanggungjawab untuk meneliti kesahihannya dari sudut Perlembagaan.
Justeru, mengekalkan Akta Hasutan semata-mata kerana ia sudah lama wujud, pada pandangan saya, tidak memadai tanpa penelitian terhadap kesesuaiannya dengan kerangka Perlembagaan hari ini.
Perkembangan keputusan mahkamah tertinggi mengenai keluhuran Perlembagaan dan kuasa kehakiman membuka ruang untuk kedudukan Akta Hasutan dinilai semula secara menyeluruh.

Jika mahkamah akhirnya mendapati akta itu bercanggah Perlembagaan, mengetepikannya bukan sahaja akan menamatkan satu tinggalan undang-undang zaman penjajah, malah menegaskan komitmen negara terhadap pemerintahan berasaskan Perlembagaan sendiri.

Ia juga akan memperlihatkan badan kehakiman bukan sekadar menunaikan sumpah jawatan, tetapi melaksanakan tanggungjawabnya dalam mempertahankan kedudukan Perlembagaan sebagai undang-undang tertinggi negara.

f580bac90f01a7b8: JERUSALEM: Gaza's civil defence agency said that Israeli fire on Tuesday killed at least seven people, including a Hamas commander, confirming an earlier report from the Israeli military.
The agency, which operates as a rescue force under Hamas authority, said that Izz al-Din al Beik was killed in an Israeli strike west of Gaza City, together with another man.
Hamas described him in a statement as a "member of the General Military Council of the al-Qassam Brigades (Hamas's military wing) and commander of the Northern Brigade."
Announcing Beik's killing, the al-Qassam Brigades said he had been one of the commanders in the operations room for Hamas's Oct 7, 2023 attack on Israel that sparked the Gaza war.
The Israeli military confirmed Beik's role as commander of Hamas's northern Gaza brigade, and said he had directed Hamas operatives to carry out attacks against Israeli troops and civilians.
He was "eliminated in a precise aerial strike", the military said.

The civil defence further reported that three people were killed and several injured in two Israeli drone strikes in the Jabalia area in the northern Gaza Strip, and one person was killed by Israeli gunfire in Deir al-Balah in the centre of the territory.
Later on Tuesday evening, another person "was killed and others were wounded in an Israeli drone strike targeting a house" in Gaza City, the civil defence agency reported.
When contacted by AFP, the Israeli military said it would later provide further details about some of the targets.

The massive Israeli offensive in response has left most of Gaza in ruins and killed more than 74,000 people, according to Gaza's health ministry, which is under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
Israeli forces have killed more than 1,400 people since a ceasefire was announced last October, according to Gaza's health ministry.
The Israeli military has identified five deaths in its ranks over the same period, as well as the death of one civilian contractor.--AFP
6add1e56b5f3de8d: SEPTEMBER 30 — I recently came across a sight that is becoming increasingly rare.
In an open field in Taiping, rows of freshly washed clothes hung from simple poles and clotheslines, moving gently in the afternoon breeze.
Towels, blankets, shirts, trousers and large pieces of cloth stretched beneath the open sky, drying naturally under the warm sunlight.
There were no tumble dryers humming in the background. Just sun, wind and time.
I stood there for a while, watching the clothes sway quietly, and found myself thinking about how differently we once approached something as ordinary as washing clothes.
For most of human history, laundry was among the most physically demanding household tasks.
Clothes had to be soaked, scrubbed, rinsed, wrung by hand and finally carried outside to dry.
The repeated work of scrubbing, wringing and carrying also built physical strength, exercising muscles in ways we rarely associate with doing the laundry today.
Long before washing machines became part of everyday life, rivers and streams served as natural washing places.
Families gathered by the water, washing clothes against stones or wooden boards while exchanging news, conversation and laughter.
What we now think of as a household chore was once woven naturally into the rhythm of community life.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Freshly washed clothes sway gently in the breeze, drying naturally beneath the warm afternoon sun. — Picture by Ng Kwan Hoong
There were also the dhobis, professional laundry workers whose occupation travelled from the Indian subcontinent to many parts of South-east Asia, including Malaya.
They washed, dried and ironed clothes for households that depended on their skill and hard work.
Their trade has largely disappeared, replaced by washing machines, laundries and twenty-four-hour self-service laundromats.
Yet watching those clothes drying beneath the Taiping sky, I realised that the dhobi represents something larger than a profession that has gradually faded from view.
He belonged to a time when ordinary work was carried out in partnership with nature. The sun was not simply something to endure. It was part of the process.
The wind was not an inconvenience. It helped finish the work.
Even time itself played an important role. Clothes dried when the weather allowed them to dry, not when a programme ended or a timer sounded.
Laundry followed the rhythms of daylight, sunshine and changing skies.
Modern technology has transformed this experience beyond recognition.
Washing machines have spared us hours of physical labour. Spin cycles remove much of the water before clothes even leave the drum.
Electric dryers finish the task regardless of whether it is raining or shining outside.
These advances have undoubtedly made life easier, particularly for busy families living in cities and high-rise apartments where outdoor drying is often impractical.
Few of us would willingly return to washing every piece of clothing by hand.
Yet watching those clothes in Taiping reminded me that progress does not always require us to leave everything behind.
Sometimes it simply changes our relationship with the world around us.
When we dry our clothes outdoors, we become quietly aware of the weather.
We notice whether the morning is bright, whether clouds are gathering, whether the wind is strong enough to hasten the drying or whether rain might arrive before evening.
Without consciously thinking about it, we begin paying attention to the natural rhythms that have always surrounded us.
Modern appliances have given us something valuable: freedom from much of the physical effort that once consumed an entire day.
But they have also made many everyday tasks wonderfully invisible.

We load the machine, press a button and return later when everything is finished. The washing is completed while we attend to other things, scarcely noticing the passing of time or the changing sky outside our windows.
There is nothing wrong with that. Technology should make our lives easier. That is precisely what good technology is meant to do.
The more interesting question, perhaps, is whether convenience should also disconnect us from the natural world that quietly sustains us.
Throughout my years in science and engineering, I have often been reminded that the most elegant solutions are not necessarily those that overpower nature, but those that work harmoniously with it.
A sailboat moves because it understands the wind rather than resisting it.

Solar panels harvest sunlight that arrives freely each day. Even the simple clothesline reminds us that some of the most effective technologies have always worked alongside nature rather than trying to replace it.
As I left the field in Taiping, the clothes were still moving gently in the breeze.
Before long they would be dry, just as they had been for generations before electric dryers, automated laundries and the convenience of modern appliances.
Watching them, I realised that Nature was quietly finishing the work.

Perhaps that is something worth remembering. Not because we should abandon the remarkable technologies that have improved our lives, but because progress is at its best when it helps us live more wisely with the world around us, rather than forgetting it was there in the first place.
Sometimes, all it takes is just sun, wind and time.

* Ng Kwan Hoong is an Emeritus Professor of Biomedical Imaging at the Faculty of Medicine, Universiti Malaya. A 2020 Merdeka Award recipient, he is a medical physicist by training but also enjoys writing, drawing, listening to classical music, and bridging the gap between older and younger generations. He may be reached at ngkh@ummc.edu.my

bde4d13ce766dbdd: COPENHAGEN, Sept 30 — Uefa chief Aleksander Ceferin on Tuesday attacked Fifa president Gianni Infantino, saying “football has no need for emperors”, while powerful Paris Saint-Germain president Nasser al-Khelaifi insisted he has no interest in becoming the next head of global football.

“Yes, let’s grow, let’s innovate, let’s make our clubs and competitions even more successful, but let’s never forget that football is bigger than those who govern it. We are custodians, we are not owners. Nobody has the right to sell its future,” Ceferin, the leader of European football’s governing body, told the European Football Clubs (EFC) general assembly in Copenhagen.

Uefa, whose clubs and national teams dominate football’s global economy, has been outspoken in its opposition to Infantino ever since it emerged in late July that Fifa was aiming to create a commercial subsidiary called Fifa Forward Enterprise to run its biggest events, such as the World Cup and Club World Cup.

It said it would consider boycotting Fifa-organised tournaments before suspending that threat after receiving written assurances in late August that world football’s governing body would not try to revive the plans to sell stakes to private investors.

Uefa has also gone to a court in the US state of Florida in an attempt to access documents related to Infantino’s failed plan with the aim of gathering evidence for a potential criminal complaint in Switzerland — Uefa and Fifa are both based there.
The latter has responded to that by accusing the European body of a “misinformation campaign” and saying Uefa was attempting to “influence” the Fifa presidential election scheduled for next year.
Ceferin used his address to delegates of the powerful EFC organisation in the Danish capital to liken Infantino to the emperor in the Hans Christian Andersen fairy tale The Emperor’s New Clothes.
“We all know the story. An emperor is persuaded that he is wearing magnificent clothes, clothes which he thought only the foolish or unfit could not see,” Ceferin said.
“His court goes along with it until a child says aloud what everyone can see — the emperor is naked.
“Perhaps the moral of this story is that convenient words cannot change uncomfortable realities.”
“My friends, I think it is time to say ‘enough’,” he added, with Infantino not in attendance but Fifa general secretary Mattias Grafstrom in the room.
“Money can help the game grow, but it should never decide what we let go, never. Europe should make no apology for saying so.”
Khelaifi ‘zero interest’ in Fifa role
Numerous leading European national associations have withdrawn their support for Infantino in his bid to be re-elected president of Fifa next year.
Khelaifi, who is close to Ceferin, has been mooted as a potential candidate to stand against Infantino in the election to be held at the Fifa Congress in the Moroccan capital Rabat in March.
The Qatari president of PSG has been chairman of EFC, formerly the European Club Association, since 2021. It is through that position that he sits on the Uefa Executive Committee.
The deadline for candidates to submit their nominations is November 18, but the 52-year-old Khelaifi dismissed suggestions he might stand.
“I have zero interest in FIFA, zero ambition to be there,” he told reporters in his role with EFC, whose membership is made up of over 900 clubs across the continent.
“I don’t think I am the right guy and I don’t want to go actually. I am enjoying what I am doing and having fun. We want to continue building positive things together. Fifa is not for me.”
Khelaifi earlier used a speech to lament that time was being wasted dealing with the crisis at the top of global football.
“Football works when we listen to each other, when we are transparent,” he said. “Football is bigger and more important than any one of us.”
He also backed Ceferin to stand again to be re-elected president of Uefa next year, saying “we need strong leadership like you to protect our sport”.
Ceferin, from Slovenia, has been in his position since 2016 and has previously indicated that he would not seek re-election when his current term ends. — AFP
751c9ea72e84810d: KUALA LUMPUR: Former Felda director-general Datuk Faizoull Ahmad pleaded not guilty today to a charge of cheating the agency's board of directors into approving a power of attorney that resulted in the transfer of ownership of 16 Felda land parcels in 2014.

03864a25115d097c: KUALA LUMPUR: Muar member of parliament Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman has chosen to remember the late Tun Dr Siti Hasmah Mohamad Ali by celebrating her life, love and contributions to the country rather than through tears alone.
In a social media post, he said people had different ways of dealing with loss and grief, but what mattered most was the intention behind how they chose to do so.
"Everyone grieves differently. What matters most is the intention. Because in the end, this is not about us," he said on Instagram.

Syed Saddiq said Dr Siti Hasmah's passing was not merely the loss of a prominent figure, but also the end of an extraordinary love story between two people who complemented each other throughout their lives.

He described the relationship between the late Dr Siti Hasmah and Tun Dr Mahathir Mohamad as more than love, saying it was a lasting friendship and companionship that endured until the end of their lives.
"And perhaps, when love itself is no longer enough to describe it, it becomes something deeper — companionship.
"A life companion. A companion in the struggle. A companion until the end of life," he said.
At the same time, Syed Saddiq remembered Dr Siti Hasmah as a woman who spent her life making those around her feel valued, loved and special.
He said she also continued to serve those in need regardless of their background.
"This is also the story of a woman who spent her life making those around her feel valued, loved and special, while continuing to serve those in need, regardless of who they were.
"So, I choose to grieve in a different way," he said.
Syed Saddiq said he chose to remember Dr Siti Hasmah not solely through sadness, but by celebrating the life she lived, the love she gave and the legacy she left behind in Malaysia.

"I choose to remember Tun (Dr Siti Hasmah) not only with tears, but by celebrating the life she lived, the love she gave and the indelible mark she left on the pages of Malaysia's history and in all our hearts," he said.
72f0b82435f9236a: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 30 — Sony Pictures has unveiled the official poster for Ramayana: Rise of a Legend, offering a fresh look at the upcoming Hindi-language epic ahead of its November release.
Directed by Nitesh Tiwari, the two-part adaptation stars Ranbir Kapoor as Rama, Yash as Ravana and Sai Pallavi as Sita.
Ramayana: Rise of a Legend — Part 1 is set to open in Malaysia on November 5 and will be presented in IMAX and other premium large formats.
The film is based on the Ramayana, one of India’s best-known ancient epics, which chronicles the life and adventures of Prince Rama, an incarnation of the Hindu god Vishnu.
Traditionally attributed to the sage Valmiki, the Sanskrit epic comprises roughly 24,000 verses divided into seven books, known as kandas.
The project was first announced in 2017 as a live-action adaptation and was initially conceived as a trilogy.
A post shared by Sony Pictures Malaysia (@sonypicturesmy)
After several years of development and script refinement, it was reworked as a two-part film series under Tiwari’s direction.
With a reported budget of around ₹4,000 crore, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend has been described as one of the most expensive Indian film projects ever mounted.
The first trailer, released worldwide earlier this year, offered glimpses of Ravana’s introduction, Rama’s exile and several large-scale battle sequences.
The footage also featured a reimagined Pushpak Vimana, the flying chariot from the epic, set against a sweeping cosmic backdrop.
Tiwari co-wrote the screenplay with Shridhar Raghavan, while Namit Malhotra serves as producer.
Malhotra is the founder of visual effects company DNEG, whose credits include The Odyssey, Dune, Interstellar and Inception.
The production brings together visual effects artists who have worked on major Hollywood films, with the epic also set to be presented in 3D.
Tiwari previously directed Dangal, the 2016 sports drama starring Aamir Khan that became one of the highest-grossing Indian films worldwide.
The score is composed by Academy Award winners Hans Zimmer and A.R. Rahman.
The film is expected to screen worldwide in multiple languages, including English and Tamil, with screenings also planned for Malaysia.
Ramayana: Rise of a Legend — Part 1 is set to open in Malaysia on November 5, coinciding with the Diwali period, and will be presented in IMAX and other premium large formats.

efe6410424f8073b: SEOUL, Sept 30 — Kim Jong Un’s powerful sister denied a South Korean claim that North Korea was apparently behind landmine blasts last week that injured three soldiers, state media reported Wednesday.

The assertion over the explosions in the countries’ Demilitarised Zone “is too low and dirty as befitting the tribes of the ROK,” Kim Yo Jong said in a statement Tuesday, the KCNA news agency said, referring to the South’s formal name, the Republic of Korea.
One soldier lost a foot due to the September 21 explosions in the Demilitarised Zone, or DMZ, the heavily mined buffer zone that has divided the two Koreas since their 1953 armistice.
It is one of the world’s most heavily fortified frontiers and landmine incidents have previously heightened tensions between the two Koreas.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war since the Korean conflict ended in a truce, not a peace treaty.
After carrying out an investigation into the incident, the South Korean Defense Ministry said it concluded that North Korean mines were “highly suspected” of causing the two explosions.
“This is a clear violation of the armistice agreement, and since North Korea bears responsibility, we will take corresponding measures,” South Korean Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul said Tuesday.
But Kim Yo Jong said the South is “cooking up” bogus allegations as a pretext for political and military provocation against North Korea, KCNA said.

Since 2024, after North Korean leader Kim Jong Un designated South Korea as his country’s “principal enemy,” Pyongyang’s military has laid mines and built anti-tank barriers along the frontier as part of efforts to permanently seal it off.
During the operation, Pyongyang also blew up the northern parts of inter-Korean roads no longer in use.
Kang said Tuesday that the North Korean mines linked to the September 21 incident were believed to have been laid as part of Pyongyang’s border fortification work.
In a 2015 incident, two South Korean soldiers were seriously wounded in a landmine blast on the southern side of the DMZ, with one losing both legs.
Seoul concluded that North Korean troops had crossed the Military Demarcation Line to plant the mines, an accusation Pyongyang denied.
The incident prompted South Korea to resume anti-Pyongyang loudspeaker broadcasts along the border. — AFP
852a6080b4a50366: SINGAPORE, Sept 30 — The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has appointed five asset managers under its S$6.5 billion (about RM20.7 billion) Equity Market Development Programme, with S$1.45 billion to be placed with the managers to support the city-state’s equities market, reported Xinhua.
The five managers are Amundi, Franklin Templeton, HSBC Asset Management, M&G Investments and Natixis Investment Managers, the MAS said in a statement on Tuesday.
The latest allocation brings total placements under the programme to S$5.4 billion across 14 asset managers.
The managers will use their global distribution networks to attract international capital seeking exposure to Singapore and the region, helping broaden participation in Singapore’s equities market.
The MAS said it is reviewing proposals for a fourth batch of asset managers and expects to complete the review in 2027. — Bernama-Xinhua
4e0181e05bee57b6: SINGAPORE, Sept 30 — Public transport fares in Singapore will increase by seven per cent overall beginning December 26, 2026 amid rising energy prices due to the West Asia conflicts, the Public Transport Council (PTC) said.
In its 2026 Fare Review Exercise (FRE) report released on Tuesday, the PTC said the increase is less than half the maximum allowable fare adjustment quantum.
The council said it had sought to balance the need to keep the public transport system financially sustainable against cost-of-living concerns.
According to the 2026 FRE, adult commuters using a card will pay up to 13 cents extra per journey, while students, seniors, and persons with disabilities will pay five cents extra.
For cash payments, adults will pay an extra 20 cents, while others will pay 10 cents extra.
PTC Chairperson Janet Ang said the council is aware that every fare adjustment matters to commuters, especially when households are managing higher day-to-day expenses.

“In determining this year’s fare adjustment, PTC sought to keep the increase manageable for commuters, while balancing the need to sustain the quality and reliability of our public transport system in the face of higher costs.

“Ultimately, our responsibility is to keep public transport affordable for commuters today, while ensuring that our public transport system is of high-quality and is financially sustainable for the years ahead,” she said on Tuesday.
Meanwhile the PTC noted that the government will continue to provide additional fare subsidies amounting close to S$200 million (RM638 million) in 2027.
This is on top of more than S$2 billion in annual operating subsidies for public transport as well as capital expenditures averaging S$5 billion annually over the next five years.

“PTC will continue to monitor fare affordability closely to ensure that Singapore’s public transport system remains both affordable for commuters and financially sustainable for the long term,” it added. — Bernama

c5aefe4ed55076ee: SEPTEMBER 30 — “How old are you?”
It sounds like a simple question. But when it is directed at an adult, particularly a woman, it is often accompanied by a small disclaimer: “If you don’t mind me asking…”
That little disclaimer says more than we might realise. It suggests that we already understand age can be sensitive.
While some people may hesitate before answering or simply decline to say, others, like me, might turn the question into a joke.
Rather than simply giving a number, I sometimes say that I was born in the same year as Taylor Swift. Go figure!
Why has age become something that some of us feel the need to hide? A number is simply a measure of how many years we have lived.
However, it can carry expectations about how we should look, behave, and even what we should have achieved in life.
In Malaysia, we have a particularly interesting term for older adults: Warga Emas. Literally associated with “golden” people, the expression conveys a sense of value and respect.
Yet, the way we think and talk about ageing does not always reflect this positive idea.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
People dance at Piazza Testaccio in Rome, Italy on August 13, 2026. — AFP pic
Growing older can still be associated with decline, dependency, reduced attractiveness, or becoming less relevant.

Perhaps, this is also why some people hesitate to reveal their age. They may not be embarrassed by the years they have lived but may simply be uncomfortable with the assumptions society attaches to those years.
I was reminded of this recently when I heard about an older woman’s uncomfortable experience on public transport.
She is in her sixties, which makes her a senior citizen on paper. She is therefore entitled to senior citizen privileges, such as discounted public transport fares and priority seats.
Yet she looks considerably younger than her age. When this woman took a priority seat she was entitled to use, she received uncomfortable attention from other passengers.

A train service worker also checked her identification card and then looked at her twice. It seemed that her appearance did not immediately match their expectations of what a senior citizen should look like, or perhaps what someone receiving senior privileges should look like.
The incident made me realise that we do not merely ask people how old they are. We also expect their appearance to confirm the answer.

So, what does “old” actually look like? We seem to carry an unwritten picture of what an older person is supposed to look like: grey hair, wrinkles, modest clothing, slower movements, hunched back posture, and a walking stick.
These visual cues can become so strongly associated with ageing that when someone does not fit them, we notice.
We may even find ourselves surprised when a person tells us their age because they do not look the way we expect someone of that age to look.
Nevertheless, an older person can dye their hair, wear bright colours, travel independently, or spend hours on social media.
A 68-year-old can run a 15km marathon, while a 75-year-old can be perfectly comfortable with TikTok. None of these things make them less old.

This becomes especially interesting when society encourages people to look younger than they are. “Wow, you don’t look your age! What’s your secret?” is often considered one of the nicest compliments someone can receive. But why is looking younger automatically considered better?
We rarely hear someone say, “You look exactly your age! That’s awesome!”
Here lies a curious contradiction. We encourage people to resist looking old, yet when someone who is genuinely older does not look old enough, we may find it difficult to recognise them as such.
As the United Nations marks October 1 as the International Day of Older Persons, it is a timely reminder to think about what it means to create a more inclusive society for people of different ages.
Inclusivity is not only about providing services or privileges to older people. It also means recognising that a number should not determine how we see a person.
Therefore, the question should not be, “Why doesn’t this person look their age?” But we should ask ourselves: “Why do we expect age to look a certain way?”
* Dr Cherish How is a senior lecturer from the Faculty of Languages and Linguistics, Universiti Malaya, and can be reached at cherish@um.edu.my

f33fbad0761a5042: KUALA LUMPUR: VS Industry Bhd could see a re-rating as improving orders, higher plant utilisation and customer diversification support an earnings recovery, said UOB Kay Hian Research.

The firm said the electronics manufacturing services provider's established manufacturing capabilities, technical expertise and spare capacity positioned it to secure new programmes as customers diversify their manufacturing operations.
"Successful conversion of these opportunities could provide an additional catalyst for earnings growth and a potential re-rating," analysts Desmond Chong and Lee Cai Yu said in a note.

VS Industry returned to the black in the fourth quarter ended July 31, 2026 (Q4 FY26), posting a core net profit of RM21.4 million against a core net loss of RM32.9 million in the preceding quarter and RM18.4 million a year earlier.
The analysts said the result was broadly in line with their expectations but ahead of the consensus forecast of a RM32 million core net loss for FY26.
For FY26, revenue fell four per cent year-on-year to RM3.7 billion, mainly due to softer orders from key customers amid subdued consumer sentiment.

Excluding RM32.9 million in exceptional items, VS Industry recorded a core net loss of RM16.6 million for the year, although its fourth-quarter return to profitability marked an improvement from losses in the first nine months.
The Q4 recovery was supported by a 24 per cent quarter-on-quarter increase in revenue as orders improved at its Malaysian and Philippine operations.
The analysts said the return to profitability was partly driven by pre-festive inventory build-up and replenishment following weak orders in the preceding quarter.

VS Industry's Indonesian operations remained profitable, with FY26 pre-tax profit more than doubling to RM3.1 million from RM1.1 million, as higher orders from existing customers offset the exit of a key printed circuit board assembly customer.
Meanwhile, quarterly pre-tax losses at its Philippine operations narrowed to RM3 million from RM7 million as utilisation improved with additional models entering production.
The Philippine plant reached breakeven in August.
"The commencement of the third production line alongside a programme reportedly transferred from a competitor should provide further utilisation upside in FY27," the analysts said.
Looking ahead, VS Industry's management expects a steady recovery in customer orders ahead of the year-end festive season, with momentum likely to continue into Q1 FY27.
UOB said new model launches by key customers in FY27 should support higher plant utilisation, prompting it to raise its FY27 and FY28 earnings forecasts by four to five per cent.
The research firm maintained its "Buy" call on VS Industry and raised its target price to 35 sen from 34 sen. The stock last closed at 23.5 sen.
It said the stock's valuation remained compelling, with its current price-to-book ratio below the 0.83 to 0.88 times range seen during the Covid-19 period.
This suggested limited downside relative to the potential upside if the earnings recovery and diversification efforts translated into sustained growth.
ed5e2b26f5bd616a: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 30 — Malaysian film Irumbuth Thottam, directed by Jaydev Jayakumar, is set to become the first local Tamil feature to receive a public theatrical release in Australia.
Screenings are scheduled for October 2026, with the film presented in Australia by the Melbourne Malaysian Indian Cultural Club (MMICC).
Producer Jegen John Peter confirmed to Malay Mail that the Australian release will begin in Melbourne, with cinema listings expected to be announced soon.
Produced by AVLT Production Sdn Bhd, Irumbuth Thottam explores teenage pregnancy alongside themes of family honour and social expectations.
The crime thriller centres on the murder of a teenage girl, with two investigators tasked with uncovering the truth and identifying the person responsible.
Irumbuth Thottam was released in Malaysia on August 6 and has since completed its theatrical run, grossing RM238,876.
The film was also among the few Tamil productions to be screened in Kuala Terengganu, where, according to Jegen, it drew a large crowd, with Malays making up about 80 per cent of the audience.
Jayakumar previously told Malay Mail that Irumbuth Thottam began as a family drama before developing into a crime thriller, a genre he is passionate about.
The film was also inspired by a real-life situation the director observed during his school days.

The cast includes Irfan Zaini, Logavarman Stideran, Marie Dashani Matthews, Datuk Geethanjali G, Adli Hafidz, Balan Kash, Mohana Raj, Dhurgaashini S Vijyan, Vino Shan, Vijay Naidu, V Kogila, Kalaimamani KS Maniam and Yuneswaran Ramaraj.
The Australian screenings will give Irumbuth Thottam a theatrical audience beyond Malaysia following the completion of its domestic run.
0fc12c1747900644: HAMILTON: The US state of California has officially recognised Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, the two major Islamic holidays, under a new law signed by Governor Gavin Newsom.
Assembly Bill 2017, signed into law on Sunday, adds the holidays to the official state holiday calendar, according to Anadolu Agency.
Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan, the Islamic month of fasting, while Eid al-Adha is celebrated during the annual Haj pilgrimage.
Public schools and community colleges may close for the two holidays through existing local procedures, while eligible state employees may also receive holiday credit for them.
"The designation of Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha as state holidays is a civil calendar determination that acknowledges their cultural significance to California communities," the law stated. - BERNAMA
5c05cac242b8d4a8: TAWAU, Sept 30 — A 37-year-old Indonesian woman was reportedly found dead with injuries at a plantation workers’ quarters in Felda Umas, Jalan Kalabakan, on Monday, with police arresting her husband in connection with the case.

According to Sinar Harian, Tawau police chief ACP Rosdi Mat Jusoh said the woman, who worked at the plantation, was found unconscious following an incident at about 4.55pm and was pronounced dead at the scene at about 8.16pm.
“Investigations at the scene found injuries to the victim’s head, neck and hands,” he was quoted as saying.
Police reportedly arrested the victim’s 38-year-old Indonesian husband, who had also suffered an injury to his neck and is receiving treatment at Tawau Hospital.

Rosdi said police seized several items, including a sickle and a piece of wood, while preliminary investigations suggested the incident may have stemmed from marital problems after the couple returned from a holiday, although the exact cause remains under investigation.
He said forensic examinations, DNA analysis, medical reports and a post-mortem were being conducted, while any initial admission by the suspect would still need to be corroborated by other evidence.
The case is being investigated under Section 302 of the Penal Code and Section 6(1)(c) of the Immigration Act 1959/63.
7a37b650a88d8c4c: PETALING JAYA: Kepong MP Lim Lip Eng has voiced support for Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's efforts to seek a lasting solution to the "Myanmar refugee crisis" in Malaysia.
Lim said there were reportedly 215,600 refugees in the country registered with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees as of February, with 193,800, or nearly 90%, originally from Myanmar.
He said negotiating with Myanmar on the matter gave Malaysia a channel to urge Yangon to take responsibility and ensure the protection of repatriated refugees.
"I support Anwar’s insistence that any return must protect refugees’ safety and dignity, with clear safeguards to turn diplomatic commitments into effective protection.
"A crisis that has persisted for decades demands action. Leaving it unresolved is no solution.
"We must work towards a lasting solution now so that the next administration and future generations of Malaysians do not inherit the same unresolved crisis," he said in a statement.
The DAP veteran said countries like Germany supported the voluntary return of Syrian refugees, while providing counselling for prospective returnees seeking to reintegrate into Syrian society.
He said the UK and France also introduced an initiative in August 2025, where small-boat arrivals in France are given a legal admission route to the UK.

"These examples demonstrate the role of international cooperation and practical assistance in addressing displacement and migration. Malaysia should likewise pursue workable arrangements suited to our circumstances."
Malaysia launched the first phase of a repatriation programme yesterday involving about 5,000 Myanmar refugees, with around 1,476 sent home aboard three Myanmar naval vessels.

Anwar defended the initiative after criticism from civil society, saying Malaysia could not be expected to accommodate hundreds of thousands of refugees indefinitely without engaging Myanmar authorities on a solution.
He said Malaysia also sought to ensure that the welfare of the refugees would be ensured when Myanmar agreed to take them back.
257dccc9c9e9cd8f: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 30 — Malaysian filmmaker Woo Ming Jin’s The Fox King (Semusim Lara) has been selected as Malaysia’s official submission for the International Feature Film category at the 99th Academy Awards.

Written and directed by Woo, the Malaysia-Indonesia co-production stars Idan Aedan, Hadi Putra and Indonesian actress Dian Sastrowardoyo, and received support from the Creative Content Fund (DKK) under the Ministry of Communications through Finas.
The film had its international premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF) on September 9, 2025, where it screened in the festival’s Centrepiece programme.

It later screened at several international festivals, including the Busan International Film Festival, Jakarta Film Week, Taipei Golden Horse Film Festival, Singapore International Film Festival, Beijing International Film Festival, Far East Film Festival in Udine and the San Francisco International Film Festival.

The selection was made by the Finas Film Selection Committee, according to a statement posted by Finas on social media yesterday, based on eligibility requirements set by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS).
The 99th Academy Awards are scheduled to take place at the Dolby Theatre in Hollywood on March 14, 2027.
The Fox King centres on twin brothers Ali (Idan) and Amir (Hadi), who grow up without their mother.
Their lives change when Lara (Dian), a new English teacher, arrives and gradually becomes part of their lives, affecting the brothers’ relationship along the way.
The film joins previous Malaysian submissions in the International Feature Film category, including Emir Ezwan’s Roh and Muzzamer Rahman’s Prebet Sapu.
After completing its international festival run, The Fox King opened in Malaysian cinemas on September 17.
The Ministry of Communications and Finas also congratulated Woo, the cast and production team on the selection.
91ad242c0a3f101b: OSLO: Norway's parliament begins public hearings on Wednesday on ties between late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and Norwegian diplomats and politicians in a scandal that has shaken the nation's elite.
US president Donald Trump's Department of Justice in January released millions of Epstein-related documents, revealing connections to politicians, royals and the ultra-rich around the world.
Norway, home of the Nobel Peace Prize and often a fulcrum of international diplomacy, has seen major fallout, triggering parliamentary inquiries and police investigations.

The government must explain what it is doing to restore trust in the foreign service, said Jonas Andersen Sayed, the leader of the hearing at parliament's Committee on Scrutiny and Constitutional Affairs.
"There are many people who have demonstrated very poor judgement," Andersen Sayed told Reuters of those who had friendships with Epstein.
The committee has summoned 11 current and former foreign ministers and development ministers, including prime minister Jonas Gahr Stoere, who was foreign minister from 2005 to 2012.
Stoere has said he had no relation to Epstein.
Boerge Brende, a former foreign minister also due to testify, resigned from the position of president and CEO of the World Economic Forum after revelations of his friendly relations with Epstein.
Brende has said he was unaware of Epstein's past and criminal activities before first meeting him in 2018, and that he regretted not having investigated him more thoroughly.

Erik Solheim, a former development minister who will testify on Wednesday, has said parliament's probe is an overreaction that will throttle the foreign service as diplomats opt for needless self-restraint, harming the national interest.

Though not appearing before parliament, a number of other prominent Norwegians with ties to Epstein, including former premier Thorbjoern Jagland, former minister Terje Roed-Larsen and ex-diplomat Mona Juul, are under police investigation on corruption accusations.
All three have denied any criminal wrongdoing.

Roed-Larsen has apologised for his close relation to Epstein, which included a personal loan from the financier, and in 2020 stepped down as CEO of the New York-based International Peace Institute, a think tank.
Furthermore, Queen Mette-Marit, wife of King Haakon, has apologised for her friendship with Epstein, but is also not subject to the hearing.

In parallel, parliament has appointed an external commission of academics and legal experts to probe "matters and issues brought to light" by the files, with an aim of "improving the integrity and transparency of Norwegian authorities."

The rare investigative commission, covering more than 30 years of Norwegian diplomatic history, is due to deliver its findings in early 2028. It is only the ninth such group to be appointed by parliament in the last 140 years.
e710e3dc9fad6363: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 30 — The ringgit opened lower against major currencies including the US dollar on Wednesday as weaker US consumer data weighed on investor sentiment and reduced risk appetite in the foreign exchange market.
At 8.02am, the ringgit edged down to 4.0795/0850 against the greenback from Tuesday’s close of 4.0790/0850.
Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam said the Conference Board’s Confidence Index fell 81.9 points in September, the lowest level since April 2014.
“Based on the survey responses, most Americans related the high cost of goods and services and oil and gas prices, in particular, to such pessimism,” he told Bernama.
He added that, apart from consumer confidence, the Job Openings and Labour Turnover Survey (JOLTS) was also lower in August at 7.079 million, which was below the consensus estimate of 7.23 million.

Mohd Afzanizam said the trend has been declining since April this year. Yet the US Dollar Index (DXY) was up 0.17 per cent to 101.372 points, as US Federal Reserve officials remain hawkish on monetary policy.
At the opening, the ringgit traded lower against a basket of major currencies.

It fell against the euro to 4.6257/6320 from 4.6235/6303 at Tuesday’s close, was lower vis-à-vis the British pound to 5.3960/4032 from 5.3937/4016, and inched down versus the Japanese yen to 2.5921/5958 from 2.5869/5909.

Against Asean currencies, the local note was weaker versus the Singapore dollar to 3.1921/1969 from 3.1885/1934 at yesterday’s close and eased against the Thai baht to 12.1540/1759 from 12.1402/1632 previously.
The local note traded little changed against the Indonesian rupiah at 226.9/227.2 from 226.8/227.2 and was unchanged against the Philippine peso at 6.52/6.53. — Bernama
ac34e2b134d05834: PETALING JAYA: Malaysia perlu mencari penyelesaian berkekalan terhadap krisis pelarian Myanmar supaya masalah yang berlarutan sejak berdekad lalu tidak terus diwarisi pentadbiran dan generasi akan datang, kata Ahli Parlimen Kepong Lim Lip Eng.
Wakil rakyat DAP itu berkata beliau menyokong usaha Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim berunding dengan Myanmar bagi mencari jalan penyelesaian terhadap isu berkenaan.

“Masalah berlarutan selama beberapa dekad memerlukan tindakan," katanya dalam kenyataan sambil menekankan keperluan penyelesaian jangka panjang supaya pentadbiran dan generasi akan datang tidak terus berdepan masalah sama.
“Anak-anak kita sepatutnya mewarisi hasil kepimpinan kita, bukan akibat daripada kelewatan kita."

Lim berkata rundingan dengan Myanmar memberi Malaysia saluran untuk mendesak pihak berkuasa negara itu mengambil tanggungjawab serta memastikan perlindungan sewajarnya diberikan kepada mereka yang kembali.

“Saya menyokong ketegasan Anwar bahawa sebarang penghantaran pulang mesti melindungi keselamatan dan maruah pelarian, dengan perlindungan jelas bagi memastikan komitmen diplomatik diterjemahkan kepada perlindungan yang berkesan,” katanya.
Menurut data UNHCR setakat akhir Februari lalu, kira-kira 215,600 pelarian dan pencari suaka berdaftar dengan agensi itu di Malaysia, dengan 193,800 daripadanya berasal dari Myanmar.
Lim berkata jumlah itu menunjukkan Malaysia sudah memikul tanggungjawab besar dalam menangani krisis berkenaan dan negara memerlukan sokongan bermakna daripada masyarakat antarabangsa.
Beliau turut merujuk pendekatan beberapa negara maju dalam menangani isu migrasi, termasuk perjanjian “one-in, one-out” antara United Kingdom dan Perancis yang diperkenalkan pada Ogos tahun lalu.
Perjanjian itu melibatkan penghantaran pulang pendatang tertentu yang tiba di Britain menggunakan bot kecil ke Perancis, dengan laluan kemasukan sah ke Britain disediakan sebagai pertukaran.

Lim turut memetik langkah Jerman menyokong kepulangan secara sukarela ke Syria, termasuk menyediakan khidmat kaunseling bagi membantu mereka memahami keadaan di negara itu dan membuat persediaan untuk kembali.

Semalam, Malaysia memulakan fasa pertama program penghantaran pulang kira-kira 1,500 pelarian Myanmar, yang merupakan sebahagian daripada kira-kira 5,000 orang yang dilaporkan bersetuju untuk pulang secara sukarela.
